section.title: Rules for Christian Households
section.sectionRationale: The new life in Christ must reshape the most ordinary relationships, so Paul applies it to the first-century household: wives and husbands, children and fathers, slaves and masters. Each pair receives a word, and every instruction is anchored in the Lord, in the Lord, pleasing to the Lord, fearing the Lord, serving the Lord Christ. The longest word goes to slaves, whose humble work is to be done for Christ, and the code ends by reminding masters that they too answer to a Master in heaven. The gospel of chapter three now walks into the home.
section.thesis: The risen life of Christ transforms the household, so that wives and husbands, children and fathers, slaves and masters each live out their relationships as unto the Lord, working sincerely for Christ who shows no favoritism and rewards His servants, while masters remember they too have a Master in heaven.
section.frameNote: Three movements: wives and husbands, in mutual submission and love; children and fathers, in obedience and gentleness; and slaves and masters, the longest word, calling for wholehearted work as for the Lord Christ who judges without favoritism, and reminding masters of their own Master in heaven.

units.label: Wives and husbands
units.note: submission and love in the Lord

verses.text: Wives, {{hypotasso|submit}} to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord.
Husbands, love your wives and do not be harsh with them.
Children, obey your parents in everything, for this is pleasing to the Lord.
Fathers, do not provoke your children, so they will not become discouraged.

units.label: Slaves and masters
units.note: working as for the Lord Christ, who shows no favoritism

verses.text: Slaves, obey your earthly masters in everything, not only to please them while they are watching, but with sincerity of heart and fear of the Lord.
Whatever you do, work at it with your whole being, as for the Lord and not for men,
because you know that you will receive an {{kleronomia|inheritance}} from the Lord as your reward. It is the Lord Christ you are serving.
Whoever does wrong will be repaid for his wrong, and there is no {{prosopolempsia|favoritism}}.
Masters, supply your slaves with what is right and fair, since you know that you also have a Master in heaven.

hypotasso.gloss: To arrange under, to submit or order oneself under another, originally a military term for ranking under an order. Wives are called to submit to their husbands as is fitting in the Lord, a voluntary ordering, not servility, that mirrors the church's response to Christ. It is set within a code where husbands are commanded to love, so authority is never a license for harshness.

kleronomia.gloss: An inheritance, a portion received as an heir. Strikingly, Paul promises the inheritance to slaves, who by Roman law could own and inherit nothing, telling them their true reward comes from the Lord. In Christ the lowest servant is a full heir of God, which utterly reframes their daily labor as service rendered to the Lord Christ.

prosopolempsia.gloss: Partiality or favoritism, literally the receiving of a face, judging by outward status. Paul says the Lord shows no favoritism: masters get no special treatment and wronged slaves are not overlooked. The same impartial Judge reckons with everyone, which both comforts the mistreated servant and warns the powerful master.

basic.context: The new life of chapter three now enters the home. Paul speaks to the three pairs that made up a first-century household: wives and husbands, children and fathers, slaves and masters. To each he gives a short, pointed word, and he keeps tying every duty to Christ: do this as is fitting in the Lord, pleasing to the Lord, out of fear of the Lord. He spends the most words on slaves, telling them to work wholeheartedly for Christ, who will reward them, and he reminds masters that they too must answer to a Master in heaven.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a household code, a familiar form in the ancient world, but Paul reshapes it around Christ and makes it strikingly mutual: husbands must love, fathers must not provoke, masters must be fair. The instructions to slaves describe how to live faithfully within an existing system; they are not an endorsement of slavery, and the whole New Testament trajectory undermines it. The abiding principles are Christ-centered relationships, love, and integrity.
basic.originalLanguages: Wives are to hypotasso, to order themselves under their husbands, a voluntary submission set beside the husband's command to love. Slaves are promised a kleronomia, an inheritance, though by law they could own nothing, because their true reward is from the Lord. And the Lord shows no prosopolempsia, no favoritism, judging master and slave alike by the same impartial standard.
basic.typology: The ordering of the Christian household reflects the greater relationship of Christ and His church, which Ephesians makes explicit. The inheritance promised to slaves fulfills the hope of God's people receiving their portion, now open to the lowest servant in Christ. The impartial Judge who shows no favoritism reflects God's own justice throughout Scripture.
basic.christ: Christ is named in nearly every line: relationships are ordered in the Lord, obedience pleases the Lord, work is done for the Lord Christ, and He is the one who gives the inheritance and judges without favoritism. Even a slave's daily task becomes direct service to Jesus. Christ is Lord of the whole household, high and low alike.
basic.god: The God revealed here is perfectly just and impartial, showing no favoritism to the powerful and not overlooking the wronged. He is the Master in heaven to whom even earthly masters must answer, and the Lord who rewards faithful service with an inheritance. He dignifies the humblest worker and holds the mightiest accountable.
basic.crossReferences: Ephesians 5 and 6 give a fuller version of this same household code, grounding marriage in Christ and the church. First Peter 2 and 3 apply similar instructions to servants and spouses. And Philemon shows Paul urging a master to receive his slave as a beloved brother.
basic.oneStory: The gospel that rescues and renews now reaches into ordinary homes, reordering the closest relationships under the lordship of Christ. In Him the powerless are made heirs and the powerful are humbled before their heavenly Master, a foretaste of the kingdom where the last are first and Christ is Lord of all.

context.literary:
The passage is a household code, a compact unit of nine verses with a very regular design. Three pairs are addressed in turn, and in each pair the second party is spoken to as directly as the first. Wives, husbands. Children, fathers. Slaves, masters. Each address has the same three parts: the person named, a command, and a reason or limit attached to the command. The shape is so even that readers have long sensed that Paul is working from a recognized form and deliberately reshaping it.

The distribution of words is the first clue to the emphasis. The first two pairs receive one verse each for the subordinate party and one for the other. The third pair is far longer: four verses for slaves (3:22 to 25) and one for masters (4:1). A reader following the length of the unit would conclude that the weight of the passage falls on the slave, because the word of Christ is hardest to see there.

A second pattern is the repetition of "Lord." It appears in 3:18, 20, 22, 23, 24 (twice) and 4:1, and in the middle of the unit the word shifts meaning, since "masters" in 3:22 and 4:1 is the same Greek word, kyrios, as "Lord." The earthly masters are literally "lords according to the flesh," and the heavenly Lord stands over them. The passage is held together by this wordplay: every human lordship is under one Lordship.

The unit also forms a hinge in the book. Chapter 3 has just said that "whatever you do, in word or deed, do it all in the name of the Lord Jesus," 3:17, and the household code is the test case, the place where the abstract principle meets the ordinary day. The prayer unit of 4:2 to 6 then turns outward again.
context.historical:
Writers of the ancient world often discussed the proper ordering of a household, and the pattern of three pairs, husband and wife, parent and child, master and slave, goes back at least to Aristotle's discussion of household management in the Politics. Later moralists, Jewish and pagan, repeated the scheme. Paul's first readers would have recognized the form. The usual codes addressed only the one with authority, telling the head of the house how to manage those under him. Paul addresses the wife, the child and the slave directly, as moral agents who answer to the Lord for themselves, which was unusual.

The Roman household was under the authority of the paterfamilias, and the law gave him wide power over wife, children and slaves. A slave had no legal standing in many matters and could be bought, sold or punished. Slaves made up a large part of the population of cities in the empire, and they included skilled people, managers and household teachers as well as laborers. Manumission was possible and common enough that freedmen formed a visible class. Some slaves were in Christian households, and some masters were themselves believers, as in the case of Philemon, to whom Onesimus belonged, Philemon 1:10 to 16. Colossians and Philemon were probably carried to Colossae by the same men, Tychicus and Onesimus, Colossians 4:7 to 9, so the original hearers of this passage may have heard it with Onesimus standing in the room.

The early church met in households, 4:15, so the house was not only the place where the code applied but also where the gathered church met. Wives, children and slaves sat in the same assembly as their husbands, fathers and masters, and heard the letter read to all of them. The first audience heard themselves addressed in the presence of one another, and that setting itself changed what the commands could mean.
context.canonical:
The passage belongs with a small family of New Testament household instructions. Ephesians 5:21 to 6:9 is the nearest, and nearly every phrase in Colossians has a longer form there. First Peter 2:18 to 3:7 addresses slaves and then wives and husbands, and 1 Timothy 6:1 and 2 and Titus 2:1 to 10 give shorter forms for particular groups. The common thread is that the gospel is expected to touch the most ordinary relationships and that the church's conduct there is a witness, 1 Timothy 6:1, Titus 2:10.

Each of the three pairs reaches back into the Old Testament. Children are told to obey as Exodus 20:12 says to honor father and mother, a command Paul quotes in Ephesians 6:2, and the wisdom books repeat it, Proverbs 6:20. The Old Testament law set limits on slavery that differ from the practice of surrounding societies: the Hebrew servant went free in the seventh year, Exodus 21:2, and Israel was told to remember that it had been a slave in Egypt, Deuteronomy 15:12 to 15. Kidnapping a person to sell him was a capital crime, Exodus 21:16, and 1 Timothy 1:10 lists slave traders among the lawless.

The foundation for the last verses is God's impartiality. Deuteronomy 10:17 says the LORD shows no partiality, 2 Chronicles 19:7 repeats it to judges, and Romans 2:11 and Acts 10:34 apply it to Jew and Gentile. Colossians 3:25 applies it in the household: the same standard of judgment for the master and the slave. Jesus' own words about authority among His followers, Mark 10:42 to 45, stand behind the mutual direction of the whole passage.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul writes to a church that has just been told that all earthly divisions are relativized in Christ, 3:11, and that the Lord Jesus is to be the name over everything, 3:17. A natural question follows: does that mean the household is now to be thrown over? Paul's answer is that the household is to be transformed from within. He keeps the ordinary structure of the home but changes the motive and the accountability. Every person is to act as under the eye of the Lord, and every person who holds power in the home is reminded that he or she answers to Him.

The first hearers would have noticed what was missing from the usual code: no praise for the master's authority and no promise that the household's order would be secured. Instead the powerful party is bound by love (husbands), restraint (fathers) and fairness (masters). The weaker party is treated as a person who can serve the Lord by choice. Paul intends the Colossians to see that following Christ in the home is not a lesser part of discipleship but one of its main tests, and that a church which gets this right will be an attractive witness among neighbors who watch how they live.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage prescribes conduct, but it does so within a social order that it does not itself prescribe. The structures of ancient households, including slavery, are the setting in which the commands are given. It does not follow that the structures are commended. The text tells slaves how to act within a situation they did not choose, tells masters to treat them rightly, and never says that the system of slavery is good or that it should last. The New Testament goes elsewhere on that, as in the praise of freedom in 1 Corinthians 7:21 and the appeal to receive Onesimus as a brother in Philemon 16.

Within the commands, some instruction is meant for all times, and some is shaped by its setting. That a husband must love his wife and not be harsh, that a father must not drive his children to discouragement, that an employer must be fair and remember he has a Master, are principles that apply wherever there are marriages, parents and workers. How submission, obedience and authority are carried out will look different in different cultures, and the text itself shows how differently it addresses the three pairs. The wise reading holds the principle firmly and asks what faithful practice looks like now, while refusing to turn a description of ancient slavery into a license for any form of oppression.

debates.question: What does 'wives, submit to your husbands' ask, and how far does it reach?

views.label: A distinct role of headship and submission
views.case: The command is addressed to wives only, and similar teaching is in Ephesians 5:22 to 24, 1 Peter 3:1 to 6 and Titus 2:4 and 5, where it is grounded in the order of creation and the relation of Christ and the church. 1 Corinthians 11:3 speaks of headship. On this reading the husband bears a loving responsibility to lead and the wife willingly places herself under it, while the command to love and not be harsh limits how that leadership is used.

views.label: Mutual submission shaped by love
views.case: Ephesians 5:21 introduces the whole code with 'Submit to one another out of reverence for Christ,' and in 1 Corinthians 7:3 and 4 husband and wife have the same claim on each other. On this view the distinctive command to wives is an instance of the general call to yield, and the weight of the passage lies on the husband's self-giving love, which in Ephesians 5:25 is as costly as Christ's.

views.label: A cultural form being redirected
views.case: Some argue that Paul takes up the household order of his day and reshapes it, so that its pattern is not permanent but its principle, love and humility, is. They point to the fact that the household codes also address slaves and masters, and that the church has not taken the slave section as a timeless rule.

debates.bearing: The three views agree on the limit that Paul sets: the submission is 'as is fitting in the Lord,' and it is paired with a command that forbids harshness. Whichever reading is held, the passage rules out domination and asks the husband to measure himself by the cross.

debates.question: Does Paul endorse slavery by telling slaves to obey?

views.label: He accommodates an existing order and undermines it
views.case: The text instructs, but it never defends the institution. It treats slaves as persons answerable to the Lord, promises them an inheritance, and calls masters to fairness. Philemon 16 asks that a slave be received as a brother, and 1 Corinthians 7:21 encourages freedom when it is available. On this view the gospel quietly removes the foundations of slavery while teaching Christians to behave well within it.

views.label: He accepts it as a feature of the age
views.case: Some argue that Paul has no program against slavery and writes within the assumptions of his time, which should be acknowledged honestly. Defenders of this reading say the passage must be applied by principle, not copied, and that its use to defend slavery in later centuries was a serious misreading, since it ignores Exodus 21:16 and the reversal of rank in the church.

views.label: He applies a gospel that works outward over time
views.case: A third view holds that the gospel sets a principle, one Master over all and equal standing in Christ, that eventually brings down slavery as it works its way through the church. Church history shows both the truth in this and the long delay, which should keep believers from pride.

debates.bearing: Whichever view is taken, the passage cannot be used to bless owning people. It takes the dignity of the slave more seriously than the culture did and puts the master on notice that he is accountable to a higher Lord. It should be read together with Philemon, Colossians 3:11 and 1 Timothy 1:10.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 18 begins with hypotassesthe, "submit," a compound of "under" and "arrange." It is a present imperative in the middle or passive voice, and the middle gives the sense of putting oneself in order, of an act that the wife herself performs. The word differs from hypakouo, "obey," which Paul uses for children and slaves in verses 20 and 22. The change suggests that Paul does not treat the wife's position as the same as a child's or a slave's. The phrase that follows, hos aneken en kyrio, "as is fitting in the Lord," uses an imperfect verb that means "was fitting" and describes a standard already established.

The husband's command in verse 19 is agapate, present imperative of agapao, "keep on loving," the verb used throughout the letter for the love that God has shown. The second half, mE pikrainesthe, is "do not be bitter" or "do not be harsh," a verb that describes a sour, embittered attitude. The one who holds power is told what he must not become.

Verse 21 uses erethizo, "provoke" or "stir up," and says that the danger is that the children athymosin, "lose heart." Ephesians 6:4 has a different word, "provoke to wrath." Colossians names the quieter damage, a child worn down until he stops trying. Both words show Paul taking children's inner life seriously.

In verse 22 Paul coins a compound, ophthalmodoulia, "eye service," and names the vice it describes with another, anthropareskoi, "men-pleasers." The same two words occur in Ephesians 6:6. Against them he sets haplotes kardias, "sincerity of heart," a simplicity of single purpose, and "fear of the Lord." Verse 23 says to work ek psyches, "from the soul," which the BSB renders "with your whole being." The Greek locates the effort in the center of the person, so that the work is not performed at half power for a human boss.

The reward in verse 24 is an antapodosis, "repayment," of a kleronomia, "inheritance." The genitive means that the repayment consists of the inheritance. In the legal world of the time slaves could not normally inherit, so the word is deliberately surprising. The same word family is used of children and heirs in Romans 8:17. Verse 25 then says that the wrongdoer komisetai, "will receive back," what he did, a verb of full payment, and that there is no prosopolempsia, "favoritism," literally "receiving a face." The word is formed from the Hebrew idiom for lifting up the face, as in Leviticus 19:15, and it names the practice of judging by rank, looks or wealth.

In 4:1 Paul asks masters to give what is to dikaion kai ten isoteta, "the right and the fair," where isotes can mean "fairness" and also "equality." The same word appears in 2 Corinthians 8:13 and 14 where it names the equality of mutual sharing. A master hearing it would have heard that the slave had a claim on him that was more than minimal. The title of the master, kyrios, is the same word as for Christ, and the final phrase, "a Master in heaven," makes the point that every kyrios is a slave to the true One.

typology.type: The family order of creation, Genesis 1:27-28 and 2:18-24
typology.fulfillment: The household begins in Genesis, where man and woman are made in God's image and given the work of ruling and filling the earth together, and where a man leaves his father and mother and is joined to his wife. Paul's code assumes this created pattern and works to restore it after the damage of Genesis 3:16. The escalation comes in Ephesians 5:31 and 32, where the marriage union is called a profound mystery that refers to Christ and the church. The correspondence is not exact, because no husband loves as Christ does; the pattern points to a love that the husband can only follow.

typology.type: The slave released in the seventh year, Exodus 21:2 and Deuteronomy 15:12-15
typology.fulfillment: Israel's law ordered that a servant go free after six years and be sent out with generous gifts, 'Remember that you were slaves in the land of Egypt.' The pattern joins the memory of redemption to the treatment of the weak. Christ extends it by freeing people from a greater slavery, so that 'you were bought at a price,' 1 Corinthians 7:23, and the freed become His servants, Romans 6:22. The type falls short in that it dealt with physical bondage within Israel, while the gospel frees from sin and brings all peoples into one family, Galatians 3:28.

typology.type: The Servant of the LORD, Isaiah 42:1
typology.fulfillment: The Servant is chosen, upheld, and brings justice to the nations. The slaves of the household code are told to serve the Lord Christ, who took 'the form of a servant,' Philippians 2:7, and who said He had come to serve and to give His life, Mark 10:45. The correspondence is that lowly service is the shape of the Messiah's mission. The escalation is that the humblest work done for Him shares in His own pattern. The type is limited, since the Servant's suffering saved others while ours only follows Him.

Israel confessed a God who shows no partiality and takes no bribe. The code's last clause, that 'there is no favoritism,' draws on this confession. Jesus embodies it as the Judge before whom 'we must all appear,' 2 Corinthians 5:10, and Acts 10:34 shows its reach to the nations. The correspondence is of a judgment that ignores rank. The pattern breaks only in this: the Judge who weighs the master and the slave is also the one who bore the penalty for both.

study.christ:
Christ is named or implied in every verse of the passage, but in a way that is easy to miss. Paul does not refer to a past event or a doctrine here; he says that the household is lived out under a living Lord. "In the Lord" in verse 18, "pleasing to the Lord" in verse 20, "fear of the Lord" in verse 22, "for the Lord" in verse 23, and "the Lord Christ you are serving" in verse 24 form a steady refrain. The Lord Jesus is present in the kitchen, the nursery and the workshop.

He is the judge who rewards. The slave will "receive an inheritance from the Lord as your reward," verse 24, and the one who does wrong will be repaid, verse 25. The same Jesus who forgave in 2:13 will weigh each life, 2 Corinthians 5:10, and this future gives the present work meaning. A task that no earthly master praises is seen by the One who matters.

He is the model for every authority that is described. A husband's love is later measured by the way Christ loved the church, Ephesians 5:25. A father's restraint reflects the Father's patience. And the master with a Master in heaven is told to act like the One who said that those who rule among the Gentiles lord it over them, but it must not be so among His followers, Mark 10:42 to 45. In John 13:14, the Lord and Teacher washes feet.

He is also the one whose lordship redefines status. Calling Jesus kyrios, as the whole letter does, meant that no other claimant could hold absolute title over anyone. Paul's repeated use of the word places every human master in a derived and temporary position. To carry this to its limit would be forced, because the passage does not tell masters to free slaves. But the direction of the language is clear, and Philemon shows how a Christian master was expected to see a slave: as a beloved brother, Philemon 16.

The passage guards against turning Christ into a decoration for the existing order. He does not bless the household as it stands; He claims it and judges it. For that reason the passage is a call to Christ-centered service, which gives dignity to ordinary tasks, and a call to Christ-shaped authority, which strips power of its claim to be used for the powerful.
study.god:
The God of this passage is impartial and just. The claim that "there is no favoritism" is the theological anchor of the whole unit, and it matches what Deuteronomy 10:17 says of the LORD: He is God of gods and Lord of lords, showing no partiality and accepting no bribe. It is meant to comfort the slave, who has no earthly judge to appeal to, and to sober the master, who cannot count on rank to protect him. The same God is on the side of the wronged and holds the powerful to account, as Proverbs 14:31 says that oppressing the poor insults the Maker.

He is a God who sees. The slave is told to serve "with sincerity of heart and fear of the Lord," and not only when watched, verse 22. This presumes a God who sees what no human overseer sees. The thing that makes the difference in work is not the audience but the awareness that the work is done before Him. This quality is also what is meant by the fear of the Lord, which in the Old Testament is the beginning of wisdom and an attitude of reverent trust, not of terror.

He is generous in rewarding. The word "inheritance" carries the idea of a gift that belongs to sons, and it is promised to those who could hold nothing of their own. This sets forth a God who gives beyond what is earned, a Father who treats the lowest servant as an heir. It matches Romans 8:17 and Colossians 1:12, where believers share in the inheritance of the saints.

God is also the Lord of ordinary life. The passage does not tell the church to leave the household to find holiness. It assumes that He is to be worshiped and served in cooking, parenting, farming and trade. This fits the creation account, where work and family are part of the good order God made, and it fits Colossians 3:17, where every word and deed falls under His name.

A final point concerns authority. The God here is one who gives authority and who limits it. Husbands, fathers and masters are not told that authority is bad, but their authority is bounded by a command to love, to refrain from provoking, and to treat fairly. His own rule is the model, as Jesus showed when He took the role of servant, Luke 22:25 to 27. For worship, the passage teaches that a life which brings God into the home and the workplace is as much an offering as a song, and that He receives obedience given in love more gladly than ritual given in pride.

crossReferences.note: The longer household code in the sister letter. It begins with 'Submit to one another out of reverence for Christ' and links the husband's love to Christ's love for the church. It shows how Paul develops the compact lines of Colossians 3:18 to 4:1, and it supplies the mutual frame within which the individual commands should be read.

Paul asks Philemon to receive Onesimus 'no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother.' The letter was probably carried together with Colossians, and it shows what Paul meant in practice by treating a slave as a person under the Lord, which gives an interpretive key to the instructions on masters in Colossians 4:1.

'Neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female.' It states the principle of oneness that the household code works inside. The two passages should be held together: equal standing in Christ, and conduct that honors the real relationships of the home.

A slave is told not to be concerned about it, but if he can gain freedom to take the opportunity; the freed person is the Lord's freedman and the free person Christ's slave. It shows that Paul did not prize slavery and that the Lord claims both groups, which matches the Master in heaven of Colossians 4:1.

The law for releasing a Hebrew servant after six years, with generous provision and the reminder that Israel was once enslaved in Egypt. It supplies the Old Testament background of Colossians 4:1, since a master who has been redeemed must treat those under him with the memory of his own redemption.

'Honor your father and mother.' It is the root of the command to children in Colossians 3:20. Ephesians 6:2 quotes it explicitly, which indicates that Paul's household teaching is built on the Ten Commandments as well as on the culture's moral advice.

Fathers are told not to provoke their children to wrath but to bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord. It adds the positive side of Colossians 3:21 and shows that a father's job is both restraint and formation.

'God does not show favoritism.' Paul uses the same principle to level Jew and Gentile, and in Colossians 3:25 he levels master and slave. The sentence has the same meaning in each place: God judges without regard to rank or origin.

The LORD is great and mighty, 'showing no partiality and accepting no bribe.' This is the source of the impartiality that Paul invokes in Colossians 3:25, and it shows that the passage's conclusion rests on God's own character.

The rulers of the Gentiles lord it over their subjects, 'but it shall not be this way among you.' Jesus overturns the model of authority that the household code works within, and He gives the reason: the Son of Man came to serve and to give His life. It explains why the code is marked by restraint in those who hold power.

Peter addresses wives and husbands in terms close to Paul's, telling husbands to honor wives as fellow heirs of the gracious gift of life. It confirms that the New Testament household teaching is shared and that the husband's duty to honor and love is as firm as the wife's to submit.

Slaves are to honor their masters so that God's name and the teaching are not discredited, and those with believing masters should serve them all the more. It supplies the witness motive implied in Colossians 3:22 and 23 and shows that the household is a place where the gospel is either adorned or dishonored.

study.oneStory:
The passage answers a question that stretches back to Genesis: how should people live together once the order of creation has been disturbed? In Genesis 1 and 2 husband and wife share the same image and the same work, and the family is the first community. Genesis 3 brings a rupture in marriage, 3:16, and soon afterward in the family and between brothers, chapter 4. The rest of Scripture is the story of God repairing human relationships along with human hearts. Slavery appears in this story as part of the fallen world's economy, regulated and restrained in Israel's law but not part of the original design.

The passage sets this in the middle of redemption. The cross has made a new humanity, 3:10 and 11, and the new humanity must now live in houses. The effect of redemption is not to abolish the household but to renew it from within, so that the ordinary acts of marrying, raising children and working become obedience to Christ. This explains why Paul is willing to speak about conduct inside an unjust system: the church lives in the old age while belonging to the new, and its conduct is a sign of what is coming.

What the passage sets up is the church's witness in 4:2 to 6. People who are watching how the Christians treat their wives, children and slaves will ask them for a reason, and the household becomes a place of testimony. It also prepares the way for the story of Philemon and Onesimus in 4:9, where the principle is tested by a specific case.

The story ends in the new creation, where the order of lordship is complete. Every master is under the Master, every power is under the Lord, and there is no longer any slave or any master, because all share the inheritance as heirs. Revelation 21 and 22 show a people who serve Him and also reign with Him, a place where the work of the household is finished and the one family of God lives in His presence. The code of Colossians 3:18 to 4:1 is how the church practices for that day, while still living in this one.

quiz.q: How does Paul balance the instruction to wives with the instruction to husbands?

options.text: Wives are to submit as is fitting in the Lord, and husbands are to love and not be harsh.
options.note: Verses 18 and 19 pair submission with self-giving love, restraining authority.

options.text: Wives must obey while husbands may do as they please.
options.note: Husbands are explicitly commanded to love and not be harsh, not to please themselves.

options.text: Both are told simply to keep the peace at any cost.
options.note: Each receives a specific, Christ-centered duty, not vague peacekeeping.

options.text: Neither is given any responsibility to the other.
options.note: Both are given clear, mutual responsibilities under the Lord.

quiz.q: Why are fathers told not to provoke their children?

options.text: So the children will not become discouraged.
options.note: Verse 21 guards children's hearts from being crushed.

options.text: So the fathers will avoid legal trouble.
options.note: The concern is the child's spirit, not the father's reputation.

options.text: So the children will fear their fathers more.
options.note: The aim is encouragement, not fear.

options.text: So the fathers can avoid all responsibility.
options.note: Fathers are given active responsibility for gentle nurture.

quiz.q: How are slaves told to do their work?

options.text: Wholeheartedly, as for the Lord and not for men, with sincerity and fear of the Lord.
options.note: Verses 22 and 23 reframe daily labor as service to Christ.

options.text: Only when the master is watching.
options.note: Paul says not only to please them while watching but sincerely for the Lord.

options.text: As little as they can get away with.
options.note: They are to work with their whole being, as for the Lord.

options.text: With resentment, since the work is beneath them.
options.note: They serve the Lord Christ, which dignifies even humble work.

quiz.q: What reward does Paul promise faithful slaves, and why is it striking?

options.text: An inheritance from the Lord, striking because slaves could legally own nothing.
options.note: Verse 24 makes the lowest servant a full heir in Christ.

options.text: Immediate freedom from their masters.
options.note: The promise is a heavenly inheritance, not automatic manumission.

options.text: Higher social rank in the community.
options.note: The reward is from the Lord, not social advancement.

options.text: Nothing; their work goes unnoticed.
options.note: Their work is seen and rewarded by the Lord Christ.

quiz.q: What does Paul remind masters of in 4:1?

options.text: That they must be right and fair, since they also have a Master in heaven.
options.note: Masters answer to their own heavenly Master, which curbs abuse.

options.text: That they may treat slaves however they wish.
options.note: They are commanded to be just and fair, not to do as they please.

options.text: That they are accountable to no one.
options.note: They are accountable to the Master in heaven.

options.text: That earthly power is all that matters.
options.note: Their earthly power is placed under God's higher authority.

questions: Paul ties every household duty to the Lord. How would consciously doing your family or work relationships for Christ change the way you treat the people closest to you?
Authority in this passage is always fenced in by love and fairness. Where do you hold some authority, and how could you exercise it with more gentleness and justice?
Slaves were told their ordinary work was service to the Lord Christ. What routine or unnoticed task could you begin to offer to Jesus as worship this week?
God shows no favoritism, honoring the lowly and holding the powerful accountable. How does that truth comfort you if you feel overlooked, or challenge you where you hold power?
Even a master answers to a Master in heaven. Who has been entrusted to your care, and how does remembering your own accountability to God shape how you lead them?

translationNotes.note: Submit renders hypotasso, a voluntary ordering of oneself under another, set within a mutual code that commands husbands to love; it does not describe servility or excuse harshness.
Earthly masters translates masters according to the flesh, distinguishing human masters from the one Lord in heaven whom all ultimately serve.
Inheritance is striking because Roman slaves could not legally inherit; Paul declares that in Christ the faithful slave receives the inheritance from the Lord as reward.
